# Caudra

**The complete coding agent for your terminal.**

Autopilot, a decision system for screening and reranking, built-in token savings, background subagents and shell calls, a learner with memory, nudges that keep small and flagship models on track, and code mode. Everything else a modern coding agent should have comes with them, designed together in one native binary.

```sh
curl -fsSL https://caudra.ai/install.sh | sh
```

On Windows, in PowerShell:

```powershell
irm https://caudra.ai/install.ps1 | iex
```

With Homebrew on macOS or Linux:

```sh
brew install caudra/tap/caudra
```

Then run `caudra` in a repository. It opens in Plan mode and writes only its plan until you approve.

Free and open source under the [Apache License 2.0](LICENSE). Runs on macOS, Linux, and Windows. Works with [17 providers](#use-the-models-you-already-pay-for), or a local model. See the [release notes](https://caudra.ai/docs/release-notes/) for the latest preview.

[Website](https://caudra.ai) · [Features](https://caudra.ai/features/) · [Documentation](https://caudra.ai/docs/) · [Quick start](https://caudra.ai/docs/quick-start/) · [Gallery](https://caudra.ai/gallery/) · [Reference configs](https://caudra.ai/docs/reference-configs/) · [Inspect the script](https://caudra.ai/install.sh)

## Step away. Autopilot keeps it moving.

*When you step away*

Autopilot answers what would otherwise wait for you, so a session keeps working toward its goal while you are away. A completion goal decides when the work is done, and your permission rules still decide what may run.

- **Engage it with one command.** `/autopilot <goal>` sets a [completion goal](https://caudra.ai/docs/commands/#completion-goals) and engages. Only you can engage it. Scripts, profiles, and the model cannot. `--autopilot` engages the session Caudra starts with.
- **Answers what would wait for you.** A separate model call, the delegate, answers permission prompts, the `question` tool, questions asked in prose, and a plan that is ready to implement. It never runs tools, and it leaves what it cannot decide safely to you.
- **Approvals that end with the call.** An approval covers one call and adds no rule. Protected files, `sudo`, and tools that always ask are never approved, and nothing is approved while [content screening](https://caudra.ai/docs/autopilot/#safety) has flagged the session.
- **Budgets and a log.** An engagement ends after 100 continuations by default, and you can cap its spend and its minutes. `/autopilot log` lists every decision, what the delegate was asked, its reason, and what followed.

Unattended work needs a running session, for example in tmux or Herdr. Closing it stops background work, and when you [reopen the session](https://caudra.ai/docs/sessions/#resuming-after-a-restart), the main turn and its subagents resume. Shell commands are not run again. When nothing screens fetched pages, engaging autopilot [says so](https://caudra.ai/docs/autopilot/#before-you-leave-it-alone). Autopilot is delegated consent and no security boundary. `/goal` looks for evidence in the transcript. It does not prove the work is correct.

[How autopilot works](https://caudra.ai/docs/autopilot/) · [More about Autopilot](https://caudra.ai/features/autopilot/) · Watch: [Work toward a goal](https://caudra.ai/gallery/#goal)

## Screen what it reads. Rank what it finds.

*When a page talks to the agent*

Caudra asks a decision model small typed questions where a judgement helps. Is this fetched page trying to instruct the agent? Which memory notes matter for this task? The answers screen what reaches the model and put what matters first.

- **Screening that can withhold a result.** [Content screening](https://caudra.ai/docs/configuration/#decisions-features) reads web, MCP, and `code` output for text that tries to instruct the agent. In `advise` mode a flagged result carries a caution. In `enforce` mode the model receives a notice in its place, and you still see the result on its card.
- **Reranking where the agent searches.** Memory search and history search keep the matches judged relevant, best first. `source_code_context` keeps the code rows that fit the task and sends no source text. Compaction keeps the results that matter to the goal, and [output pointers](https://caudra.ai/docs/configuration/#reranking) name omitted lines worth reading.
- **Advice on every prompt.** [Permission advice](https://caudra.ai/docs/permissions/#decision-engine-advice) adds warnings to a prompt without delaying it. Auto mode turns a flagged call into a prompt, and autopilot approves nothing while screening has flagged the session.
- **One endpoint you choose.** Add [TypeSafe Jev, OpenAI Luna, or a server of your own](https://caudra.ai/docs/providers/#decision-endpoints) in `/login`, and switch it in `/model`. A local server on a loopback address needs no key.

Every feature is off until you turn it on in `/decisions`, and each needs an active decision endpoint. `shadow` mode only collects predictions. The transcript shows what each feature changed, and a decision about a tool call shows on its card. Predictions add to deterministic permission rules and can miss risks. `enforce` never grants a permission, and redaction of what is sent is best effort.

[Decision endpoints](https://caudra.ai/docs/providers/#decision-endpoints) · [More about Decisions and reranking](https://caudra.ai/features/decisions/) · Watch: [Withhold a page that gives the agent orders](https://caudra.ai/gallery/#screening)

## Token savings, built in.

*When the token bill arrives*

Every turn re-sends the conversation, so a noisy result costs tokens again on every later turn until compaction. Caudra keeps results small and round-trips few, starting with RTK-style shell output filtering that is on by default.

- **RTK-style output filtering.** Command-aware rules, most of them from RTK, trim build and test noise before the model reads the output, and a filtered result is always smaller than the raw one. A failure is never reported as a success, and a failing command keeps its first and last lines. Progress bars collapse to one row, and you can switch between filtered and raw views.
- **Structure before content.** `file_index` returns a file outline with signatures and line numbers. The `source_code_*` tools rank the symbols a task touches and show callers, call sites, and the tests they can trace to a change. They parse the source on the fly, so there is no index to build or maintain and nothing to configure.
- **Fewer, smaller turns.** Oversized results reach the model as a bounded head and tail, and `tool_output` searches the rest. `batch` runs independent calls in one turn, and subagents keep their exploration out of the main context.
- **A prompt cache that holds.** MCP servers are reached through [code mode](https://caudra.ai/docs/mcp/#code-mode), so a server that connects or changes its tools never changes the tool definitions. Caudra sends a per-conversation cache key where providers accept one, and `/usage` scores the cache hit rate for every model.

With credit to the ideas in [RTK](https://www.rtk-ai.app/docs/) and [ripwire](https://github.com/redhat-et/ripwire).

[How Caudra saves tokens](https://caudra.ai/docs/token-economy/) · [More about Token savings](https://caudra.ai/features/token-savings/) · Watch: [Filter shell output](https://caudra.ai/gallery/#filter), [Answer from outlines and references](https://caudra.ai/gallery/#code), [Context and token usage](https://caudra.ai/gallery/#usage)

## Work in the background. Steer it while it runs.

*When work takes a while*

Subagents and long shell commands keep running while the main agent moves on, and their reports wake it when they finish. The input stays open the whole time, so you can queue the next task, guide the current run, or open any subagent and steer it.

- **Subagents in the background.** A [task](https://caudra.ai/docs/sessions/#background-tasks) can run in the background while the main agent works on a separate part. Its report starts the next step at a safe boundary, with no polling.
- **Shell calls in the background.** A long shell command can keep running in the background and report back when it ends. The footer shows that work is still running, and `/shells` lists each command with an ETA learned on your machine.
- **Guide a subagent directly.** Open a running subagent from `/tasks` and type. Your guidance stays visible until the subagent reads it at its next turn boundary. When the subagent is heading the wrong way, `Ctrl+X x` [replaces its current turn](https://caudra.ai/docs/queue/#task-chats) with your message.
- **Next, Guide, and Replace.** `Enter` queues a prompt for after the current run. `Ctrl+X g` adds guidance before the next model request, and `Ctrl+X x` stops the run and starts yours. Queued prompts stay editable.

[Background tasks](https://caudra.ai/docs/sessions/#background-tasks) · [More about Background subagents and shell calls](https://caudra.ai/features/background-work/) · Watch: [Guide a running subagent](https://caudra.ai/gallery/#steer), [Work starts while the model writes](https://caudra.ai/gallery/#eager), [Clarify a question with /btw](https://caudra.ai/gallery/#btw), [Answer a question later](https://caudra.ai/gallery/#deferred)

## Say it once. Caudra writes it down.

*When you repeat yourself*

When you correct the agent, cut an answer off, refuse a call, or repeat a preference, a background learner notices. It checks each finding against the project's history and writes what will still hold into your instruction files and project memory, so later sessions start out knowing it.

- **Evidence before it writes.** The learner is a read-only subagent that checks each finding against this project's past sessions. A line in the committed `AGENTS.md` needs evidence from at least two of them, and text that looks like a secret is refused.
- **Review and revert in `/learn`.** `/learn` lists each run with what it changed, what it dropped, and why. Open a run's transcript, revert one change, start a run now, or pause learning for the project.
- **Memory that outlasts the session.** The agent keeps notes on project gotchas and decisions outside your repository, and later sessions in the project start with those notes in view. Writes pass your permission checks, and reading needs no approval.
- **A view that stays small.** Older notes fold into a tree of one-line summaries that the Memory model writes in the background, so the view in each request stays within 32 KiB however many notes a project collects. The model opens a summary line when it bears on the task.

[How continual learning works](https://caudra.ai/docs/learning/) · [More about Learner and memory](https://caudra.ai/features/learning/) · Watch: [Review what Caudra learned](https://caudra.ai/gallery/#learn)

## Keep any model on task.

*When a local model stalls*

Smaller local models such as Qwen3.8-27B need more help to finish a task. Caudra nudges the model when a turn stalls, gets cut off, loops, or stops after announcing work. The rules react to what a reply did, so the same defaults work well with flagship models.

- **Nudges for stalled turns.** After an empty or cut-off reply, Caudra asks the model to continue. After “I will run the tests now” with no tool call, it asks for the work itself. The third identical tool call in a row is refused before it runs.
- **Hints when work goes in circles.** When the model repeats a tool cycle or an answer, or keeps making failed calls, a hint asks it to reconsider its approach. Hints stop at four per run by default and never reopen a finished answer.
- **Sensible defaults, tuned per model.** Every rule is on by default, and budgets cap how often each one fires. Change a threshold, a budget, or the wording of a nudge for all models, or only for one exact `provider/model-id`.
- **Every nudge in the transcript.** Each nudge appears as a dim row. Click it to read the exact text the model received.

In daily use, the `abandoned_turn` rule matched 35 of 386 final Qwen3.8-27B replies and none of 2,185 from Claude and GPT models, as [measured by Caudra's creator](#the-last-coding-agent-i-needed-to-install). A nudge is a message to the model. It cannot run or approve a tool, and every real tool call still passes through validation and your permission rules.

[Configure automatic steering](https://caudra.ai/docs/configuration/#agent-steering) · [More about Nudges](https://caudra.ai/features/nudges/) · Watch: [Nudge a turn that stopped early](https://caudra.ai/gallery/#nudge), [Refuse a third identical call](https://caudra.ai/gallery/#repeat), [Shell commands that a tool does better](https://caudra.ai/gallery/#redirect), [A hint toward relative paths](https://caudra.ai/gallery/#paths), [A reminder about open todos](https://caudra.ai/gallery/#todos), [Ask through the question tool](https://caudra.ai/gallery/#question)

## Call every server from one snippet.

*When a server ships 100 tools*

The model reaches your MCP servers, your past conversations, and the decision engine by writing Python in one `code` tool. The tool definitions never change when a server connects, so the prompt cache holds, and a snippet returns only what the model needs to read.

- **One tool for every MCP server.** The model never sees an MCP tool definition. It calls your servers from Python, and a snippet can call several tools at once. A server that connects, fails, or changes its tools never changes the tool definitions or the system prompt.
- **Filter before the model reads.** A snippet can filter, join, and summarise results before the model reads anything. Only what it prints and the value of its last expression come back, so a list of 500 issues can come back as three lines.
- **Python in an isolated worker.** `code` runs snippets in a separate worker with no file system, network, environment variables, or subprocesses. A snippet that calls nothing outside the worker runs without a prompt, and each call it makes, such as a search of your past conversations, is checked on its own. `timeoutSec` bounds the whole run, waits included.
- **Judgement inside the snippet.** [`decisions.decide()` and `decisions.rerank()`](https://caudra.ai/docs/code/#decisions-and-reranking) judge what a snippet gathered before any of it reaches the model.

Tools provided by [Workcell](https://github.com/caudra/caudra/tree/main/workcell).

[Code mode](https://caudra.ai/docs/mcp/#code-mode) · [More about Code mode](https://caudra.ai/features/code-mode/) · Watch: [Call MCP servers from Python](https://caudra.ai/gallery/#code-mode), [Compute with Python](https://caudra.ai/gallery/#python), [Search past conversations from Python](https://caudra.ai/gallery/#history)

## Stop assembling your coding agent.

*Everything else*

The rest of a modern coding agent ships in the same binary, designed and released together with the parts above. There are no third-party plugins to vet or keep up to date.

- **[Revert and history](https://caudra.ai/features/history/).** Search every past session, revert files with a preview, and fork from any message.
- **[Workbench](https://caudra.ai/features/workbench/).** A file explorer, editor, project search, and source control beside the session.
- **[Herdr and Orca](https://caudra.ai/features/hosts/).** Every session reports its state to the host and opens forks and worktrees in tabs of their own.
- **[Tools](https://caudra.ai/features/tools/).** File, shell, and web tools whose results say what they left out.
- **[Models and setup](https://caudra.ai/features/models/).** 17 providers, local models, and the instruction files, skills, and MCP servers you already have.
- **[Privacy](https://caudra.ai/features/privacy/).** Your history stays on your machine, and telemetry is off unless you run a collector.
- **[Experimental lab](https://caudra.ai/features/experimental/).** Durable workflows, VM sandboxes, and more, each off until you switch it on.

[Every feature, page by page](https://caudra.ai/features/)

## The last coding agent I needed to install.

*Why Caudra exists*

> I spend most of my working day with coding agents, and I have tried many of them. I kept adding plugins to get the features I wanted. Often I could not build the plugin I needed, because the agent had no hook in the place it needed one. A proper [`/goal`](https://caudra.ai/docs/commands/#completion-goals) mode was one of them. Keeping the plugins I did have up to date was work of its own.
>
> So I built those features into the agent itself, where they can work together. Caudra is one binary I can install in a new environment with one command, and it works with small local models as well as flagship ones.
>
> I push more than 40 billion tokens a month through it. With another agent, my local history grew by more than 2 GB a day. Caudra keeps over a month of my complete history in less than 4 GB, and a 10k-message session still loads in under a second.
>
> **Thorsten Born**, software engineer and data architect, creator and maintainer of Caudra

Measured by Caudra's creator in daily use:

| Figure | What it measures |
| --- | --- |
| **40B+** | tokens a month through Caudra |
| **<4 GB** | for over a month of complete local history |
| **<1 s** | to load or save a 10k-message session, subagents included |
| **~97%** | Anthropic prompt-cache hit rate, and about 94% on OpenAI |

**Method.** These are the creator's own measurements from daily use, not benchmarks. Timings were measured by hand. Results depend on models, projects, and hardware.

Caudra builds on ideas from these projects, with thanks:

- [RTK](https://www.rtk-ai.app/docs/): shell output filtering
- [ripwire](https://github.com/redhat-et/ripwire): code maps
- [Plannotator](https://plannotator.ai/): passage review
- [Herdr](https://herdr.dev): terminal workspaces for agents

## Use the models you already pay for.

*Bring your models and your setup*

First-class support for Anthropic and OpenAI, 17 built-in providers, local models through Ollama or llama.cpp, and custom endpoints that speak a supported API.

Anthropic · OpenAI · Google · GitHub Copilot · xAI · Mistral · DeepSeek · OpenRouter · Z.AI · Ollama · llama.cpp

- **ChatGPT.** Sign in with your ChatGPT subscription.
- **GitHub Copilot.** Sign in with GitHub, or import an existing Copilot token.
- **xAI.** Sign in with your xAI account.
- **Claude** (experimental). Sign in with your Claude subscription.

Claude subscription sign-in is experimental. Anthropic's terms limit Pro and Max subscriptions to official clients. Every provider also accepts an API key. See [Providers and sign-in](https://caudra.ai/docs/providers/).

Several accounts per provider, the instruction files, skills, and MCP servers you already have, and a model for each job: [Models and setup](https://caudra.ai/features/models/).

## Before you install

*Questions*

**What does it cost?** Caudra is free and open source under the [Apache License 2.0](LICENSE). You pay your model provider, or nothing when you run a local model.

**Which models can I use?** Sign in with ChatGPT, GitHub Copilot, or xAI. Or use an API key with one of the 17 built-in providers, or a local model through Ollama or llama.cpp. [Providers](https://caudra.ai/docs/providers/) lists them all.

**What leaves my machine?** Your prompts go to the model provider you choose. Telemetry is off unless you send it to a collector you run. A normal run also refreshes the public models.dev catalog and asks GitHub for a newer release, each at most once a day. It reaches Exa when the agent searches the web. [Privacy](https://caudra.ai/features/privacy/) has the details.

**Can it break my repository?** Caudra opens in Plan mode, where it writes only its plan until you approve. In Build mode, file edits inside the repository run freely, shell and web tools [ask first](https://caudra.ai/docs/permissions/), and deny rules always win. Caudra keeps a record of the file changes its tool calls make, so you can [revert](https://caudra.ai/docs/sessions/#file-revert) them from any message.

**Where does it come from?** Caudra is an independent fork of [Maki](https://github.com/tontinton/maki). It keeps Maki's native Rust core and adds many features such as completion goals, durable subagents, steering, revert, and the workbench. [Changes from Maki](https://caudra.ai/docs/changes-from-maki/) lists the work in detail.

**How stable is it?** Caudra is in preview and releases often. When an upgrade changes the session database or a config file, it saves a backup first, and older releases may not read the upgraded files. The [release notes](https://caudra.ai/docs/release-notes/) say what each upgrade changes.

**Who builds it?** Thorsten Born builds Caudra and uses it for his own work every day. Ask questions in [GitHub Discussions](https://github.com/caudra/caudra/discussions) and report bugs in [Issues](https://github.com/caudra/caudra/issues).

## Try it on the repository you have open.

*Your next working session*

Install Caudra on macOS, Linux, or Windows, sign in to a provider, and run `caudra` in your project.

### Install

On macOS and Linux:

```sh
curl -fsSL https://caudra.ai/install.sh | sh
```

Caudra is in preview, and the [release notes](https://caudra.ai/docs/release-notes/) name the latest version. The installer prefers a stable release and selects the newest preview while no stable release exists. It verifies the archive checksum before installing. A failed release lookup stops installation rather than switching channels.

The script installs Caudra to `~/.local/bin`. Set `CAUDRA_INSTALL_DIR` to choose another directory. If you would rather read the script first, download it, look it over, and run it yourself:

```sh
curl -fsSL https://caudra.ai/install.sh -o install.sh
less install.sh
sh install.sh
```

On Windows, in PowerShell:

```powershell
irm https://caudra.ai/install.ps1 | iex
```

This installs to `%LOCALAPPDATA%\caudra` and adds it to your user `PATH`. In Git Bash, the shell script above works too.

With Homebrew on macOS or Linux:

```sh
brew install caudra/tap/caudra
```

The [tap](https://github.com/caudra/homebrew-tap) installs the newest release, previews included, from the same archives and checksums as the installers. Update with `brew upgrade caudra`.

With Nix:

```sh
nix run github:caudra/caudra
```

Prebuilt binaries for Linux and macOS on x86_64 and ARM64, and for Windows on x86_64, are on [GitHub Releases](https://github.com/caudra/caudra/releases). To build the main branch yourself:

```sh
cargo install --locked --git https://github.com/caudra/caudra.git caudra
```

A plain `cargo install` build has no worker for the `code` tool, the isolated Python tool, because only release builds, Nix, and `make install` from a checkout embed it. The other tools work as usual.

### First steps

Connect a provider, then start Caudra in a repository:

```sh
caudra auth login
cd my-project
caudra
```

`caudra auth login` asks for a provider and a sign-in method. Inside Caudra, `/login` offers the same choices.

Caudra opens in Plan mode. There the agent reads and searches freely, writes nothing but its plan, and asks before any command it cannot prove read-only. When the plan looks right, press `Tab` to switch to Build mode. File edits inside the repository then run without asking. Shell commands and web tools still ask first, and you can remember each approval for the conversation or the project.

Instructions you already wrote for other agents carry over. Caudra reads `AGENTS.md` or `CLAUDE.md` from your repository and picks up skills from `.claude` and `.agents` folders.

A few more things to know on day one:

- `F1` lists every key.
- `/docs` opens the whole manual inside Caudra, matched to the version you run.
- `caudra --continue` resumes the most recent session in the current directory.
- `caudra --print` runs non-interactively for scripts and CI and exits when done.
- `caudra acp` lets editors that speak the Agent Client Protocol, such as Zed, drive Caudra.

## Caudra comes from caudate.

*Why the name*

Caudra, pronounced KAW-druh, is named after the caudate nucleus. This part of the brain belongs to the circuits that connect evidence and goals to action. Studies link it to learning which actions lead to which outcomes.

The name describes how Caudra works. It turns the context of your task into an action, then reads the outcome before it chooses the next one.

1. Context and intent
2. Evaluate evidence
3. Select an action
4. Execute with tools
5. Observe the outcome

Each outcome becomes evidence for the next step. The brain is only the inspiration for the name. Caudra is software, and it works toward the goal you set.

Sources: [Grahn, Parkinson and Owen, 2008](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0301008208001019), [Lau and Glimcher, 2007](https://www.jneurosci.org/content/27/52/14502), [Doi et al., 2020](https://elifesciences.org/articles/56694).

## Contributing

Caudra is under active development, and bug reports help a lot. Issues and pull requests are welcome on [GitHub](https://github.com/caudra/caudra/issues). Please read [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md) before you start on a larger change.

Ask questions in [Discussions](https://github.com/caudra/caudra/discussions/categories/q-a), and see [SUPPORT.md](SUPPORT.md) for where each kind of request goes. Everyone who takes part in the project follows the [Code of Conduct](CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md).

Caudra is a Rust workspace, and the `Makefile` holds the everyday commands. It requires GNU Make, Bash, and Python 3. On Windows, use Git Bash with GNU Make installed separately. Python defaults to `python3`, overridable with `make PYTHON=python <target>`.

```sh
make check         # type-check the workspace
make lint          # clippy, with warnings as errors
make test          # the test suite
make ci            # most application CI checks
make install       # install from your checkout, Python worker included
```

Cargo-compiling targets build the Python worker automatically. `make code-worker` is an optional warmup. Pass extra flags with `ARGS='...'`, such as `make build ARGS='--release'`. To sign in from a debug build, use `make run ARGS='-- auth login'`.

Canonical docs live in `docs/content/`, with navigation in `docs/navigation.json` and generated config examples in `docs/examples/`. The pages are compiled into the binary for `/docs`. The website is maintained separately and consumes these same sources. Application development and docs generation do not require JavaScript tooling.

## Credits

Caudra was created by [Thorsten Born](https://thorstenborn.com), who develops and maintains it. It stands on the shoulders of [Maki](https://github.com/tontinton/maki) and has grown in its own direction since the fork. The repository keeps Maki's history and includes work by Maki contributors. Caudra is independently maintained and is not affiliated with or endorsed by the original project.

The projects whose ideas Caudra builds on are listed [above](#the-last-coding-agent-i-needed-to-install). Caudra also adapts code from two projects:

- Most of Workcell's filter rules are copied from [RTK](https://www.rtk-ai.app/docs/) under the Apache License 2.0.
- The built-in `deep-research` workflow is adapted from [Grok Build](https://x.ai/news/workflows) under the Apache License 2.0.

The file, shell, web, source code, and Python tools come from [Workcell](https://github.com/caudra/caudra/tree/main/workcell), released under the Apache License 2.0 and developed in this workspace under `workcell/`. The isolated Python tool runs on [Monty](https://github.com/pydantic/monty) by Pydantic.
